section_summary: This section combines State Department and FBI correspondence about suspected Japanese intelligence collectors, consular connections, diplomatic immunity, photography of strategic sites, and travelers thought to be gathering information. It also contains citizen reports—some overtly racist or speculative—about Japanese activity, together with cross-reference sheets, a newspaper clipping, and an extended Sino-Korean Peoples’ League campaign alleging Japanese cultural propaganda in American schools, colleges, and churches. Several documents concern Masatsugu Fukuda, the Okamotos, the de Kanel family, Jesse S. Shima, and alleged Japanese agents or propagandists.

subfiles.title: Assistant Secretary’s handwritten routing note
subfiles.from: Assistant Secretary’s office
subfiles.about: A brief handwritten instruction concerns obtaining names or preparing a response.
subfiles.summary: The note is fragmentary and heavily obscured by handwriting and OCR. Its date and position indicate that it routed the following FBI inquiry within the State Department.

subfiles.title: FBI inquiry concerning E. Gitaro Kojima and Kotaro Minakuti
subfiles.from: John Edgar Hoover, Director, Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.about: Hoover asks whether Kojima and Minakuti are attached to a foreign consulate after reports that they sought to organize oil shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The two men reportedly arrived at San Francisco from Japan on February 22, 1939, and discussed forming a corporation to ship oil to Japan. Because information suggested a possible connection with the Japanese Consulate at San Francisco, the FBI requested confirmation of their official status.

subfiles.title: State Department reply on Kojima and Minakuti
subfiles.from: George S. Messersmith, Assistant Secretary of State
subfiles.to: John Edgar Hoover, Director, Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.about: Messersmith reports that State Department records show no consular connection for Kojima or Minakuti.
subfiles.summary: The reply acknowledges Hoover’s September 23 inquiry regarding the two men and possible espionage. Messersmith states that neither name appears among persons connected with foreign consulates and apologizes for the delayed response.

subfiles.title: Telegram reporting Masatsugu Fukuda’s departure for New York
subfiles.from: H. V. Johnson, transmitted by Joseph P. Kennedy in London
subfiles.to: James Clement Dunn, Department of State
subfiles.about: The telegram reports that Masatsugu Fukuda sailed from Southampton aboard the Statendam and was due in New York on October 31.
subfiles.summary: The message is marked strictly personal and confidential and refers to Johnson’s confidential memorandum no. 155. It identifies Fukuda’s cabin and provides his scheduled arrival date for surveillance purposes.

subfiles.title: London Embassy memorandum concerning Masatsugu Fukuda
subfiles.from: American Embassy, London
subfiles.about: The embassy warns that Japanese businessman Masatsugu Fukuda planned to travel to the United States and had previously been suspected of intelligence collection.
subfiles.summary: Fukuda is identified as manager of the import-export firm Iida & Company and as having lived in England since 1933. British suspicions that he collected intelligence had not been substantiated, but the embassy considered the information worth passing to Washington.

subfiles.title: Memorandum to the FBI concerning Fukuda
subfiles.from: Department of State
subfiles.to: Edwin A. Tamm, Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.about: The State Department informs the FBI of Fukuda’s voyage and requests any available information about him.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum gives Fukuda’s ship, cabin, route, and expected arrival at New York. It repeats rumors of intelligence collection and notes that the same information was being sent to naval and military intelligence officers.

subfiles.title: Memorandum to Military Intelligence concerning Fukuda
subfiles.from: Department of State
subfiles.about: The State Department advises Military Intelligence of Fukuda’s travel and possible intelligence activity.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum states that Fukuda sailed from Southampton on October 23 aboard the Statendam, due in New York on October 31. It solicits Military Intelligence information and records parallel notification of the FBI and Office of Naval Intelligence.

subfiles.title: Follow-up memorandum to London on Fukuda’s transit
subfiles.from: Department of State
subfiles.about: Washington confirms that Fukuda arrived in New York and held a sixty-day transit visa for travel to Japan through San Francisco.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum answers the embassy’s October reports. It confirms Fukuda’s October 31 arrival aboard the Statendam and notes that he already possessed a ticket to San Francisco.

subfiles.title: FBI report concerning the Okamotos and suspicious photography
subfiles.from: John Edgar Hoover, Director, Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.about: The FBI reports incidents involving Japanese men photographing buildings and New York Harbor and asks whether an Okamoto is a Japanese government representative.
subfiles.summary: The report describes police questioning, photographs of unidentified buildings, an automobile linked to New York, and a Japanese photographer who fled after taking pictures of New York Harbor from the Manhattan Bridge. Immigration records for Shigeo Okamoto are also summarized. Hoover asks whether the subject has official Japanese status and possible immunity.

subfiles.title: State Department reply concerning Shigaru, Shigoru, Shigeo, and Kaoru Okamoto
subfiles.from: George S. Messersmith, Assistant Secretary of State
subfiles.to: John Edgar Hoover, Director, Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.about: Messersmith advises that the investigated Okamoto appears unrelated to the Japanese consular clerk Kaoru Okamoto and probably lacks diplomatic immunity.
subfiles.summary: Department records list Kaoru Okamoto as a clerk at the Japanese Consulate General in New York since January 1936. The reply finds no evident connection between him and Shigaru or Shigoru Okamoto and notes uncertainty about the relationship to Shigeo Okamoto. It authorizes the FBI to continue investigating absent evidence of Japanese government employment.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of the George Nishisaka espionage report
subfiles.from: George S. Messersmith, Assistant Secretary of State
subfiles.to: John Edgar Hoover, Director, Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.about: Messersmith acknowledges receipt of Special Agent Emory E. Bundy’s report in the George Nishisaka espionage case.
subfiles.summary: The letter is a brief formal acknowledgment of Hoover’s November 14 communication. No findings from the enclosed report are reproduced in this section.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of the Jesse S. Shima spy-ring report
subfiles.from: George S. Messersmith, Assistant Secretary of State
subfiles.to: John Edgar Hoover, Director, Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.about: Messersmith acknowledges receipt of an FBI letter concerning Jesse S. Shima and an alleged Japanese spy ring.
subfiles.summary: The acknowledgment refers to Hoover’s November 16 letter and the case title naming Shima and aliases. It contains no substantive evaluation of the allegations.

subfiles.title: Routing note and Washington Star clipping about Jesse S. Shima
subfiles.from: Assistant Secretary’s office and Washington Star
subfiles.about: A routing note adds a newspaper account of Jesse Shima’s imprisonment and civil litigation to the espionage file.
subfiles.summary: The clipping says Shima remained in District Jail because he could not post a $500 ne exeat bond after falling behind on alimony. It recounts his inheritance from Mary F. Henderson, a failed Connecticut restaurant venture, competing lawsuits, and the court-ordered restriction on the remaining estate funds.

subfiles.title: File disposition sheet for registration material
subfiles.from: Department of State records office
subfiles.about: A brief notation records the disposition of file item 894.20211/263 to another registration file associated with Schreiner.
subfiles.summary: The page contains only the file number and a transfer or cross-filing instruction. It preserves the sequence of the decimal file but supplies no substantive case information.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on Tomemori Nakano and Shigeo Tajika
subfiles.from: Goforth, Mexico post
subfiles.about: The sheet cross-references a report on Nakano and Tajika’s trip to Mexico, Tajika’s trading-company connection, and a Japanese letter found on Nakano.
subfiles.summary: The referenced despatch reportedly included a newspaper clipping and a photographic copy of a Japanese letter mentioning Standard Oil Company and Wilmington. It also associated Tajika with Okura & Company and noted both men’s return to the United States.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of the Hattori–Takeda espionage report
subfiles.from: George S. Messersmith, Assistant Secretary of State
subfiles.to: John Edgar Hoover, Director, Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.about: Messersmith acknowledges receipt of Special Agent E. F. McCarthy’s report on Takahisa Hattori and Jiro Takeda.
subfiles.summary: The short letter thanks Hoover for forwarding the report in the named espionage case. It provides no details of McCarthy’s findings.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on Kosaku Mizusawa
subfiles.from: Department of Justice
subfiles.about: The sheet records an allegation that Japanese Minister Kosaku Mizusawa was connected with the Japanese Foreign Office Intelligence Bureau.
subfiles.summary: Mizusawa was reportedly planning to visit Chicago, Washington, and New York before returning to Panama. The source alleged that the journey’s purpose was to give new instructions to Japanese agents.

subfiles.title: State Department reply concerning James Zamends, Mr. Sato, and similarly named officials
subfiles.from: George S. Messersmith, Assistant Secretary of State
subfiles.to: John Edgar Hoover, Director, Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.about: The Department answers an FBI inquiry about whether a person in the James Zamends and Mr. Sato espionage case held an official Japanese position.
subfiles.summary: State Department records disclosed no matching officer at the Japanese Consulate General in New York. The reply distinguishes other similarly named Japanese officials or agents, including Izko Saito in Portland and registered tourism agent Shoji Osato in New York. A copy of Osato’s foreign-principal registration was sent to the Justice Department.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of the Sada Yoshime espionage case
subfiles.from: George S. Messersmith, Assistant Secretary of State
subfiles.to: John Edgar Hoover, Director, Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.about: Messersmith acknowledges Hoover’s letter concerning the Sada Yoshime espionage case.
subfiles.summary: This is a brief receipt letter referring to Hoover’s December 2 communication. It gives no facts about the alleged espionage beyond the case title.

subfiles.title: London Embassy memorandum concerning Basil E. de Kanel
subfiles.from: American Embassy, London
subfiles.about: British authorities report that alleged Japanese agent Basil E. de Kanel was in contact with a person at 819 West 180th Street in New York.
subfiles.summary: The source described de Kanel as a White Russian working secretly for Japan in the Far East. Although the contact might be only familial, British officials suggested discreet inquiries and asked to receive any resulting information.

subfiles.title: Interim memorandum on Mary de Kanel
subfiles.from: Department of State
subfiles.about: An interim investigation identifies the New York contact as Mary de Kanel and summarizes her family, medical, relief, and immigration history.
subfiles.summary: Mary de Kanel is described as a Manchuria-born social worker associated with the Children’s Aid Society and as the wife of Efrem de Kanel. The memorandum traces her nursing and relief work through Tientsin, Chita, Crimea, Constantinople, Berlin, and New York and identifies her children, including Basil and Vladimir. It also records a recent letter from “Saparva” in Chilworth, Surrey.

subfiles.title: Dunn’s request for an FBI investigation of M. de Kanel
subfiles.from: James Clement Dunn, Adviser on Political Relations
subfiles.to: John Edgar Hoover, Director, Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.about: Dunn requests discreet information about the New York correspondent of alleged Japanese secret agent Basil E. de Kanel.
subfiles.summary: The letter supplies the West 180th Street address and explains the reported link to a White Russian agent in the Far East. Dunn emphasizes the matter’s delicacy and recognizes that the relationship may be purely familial.

subfiles.title: Final memorandum to London on Mary de Kanel
subfiles.from: Department of State
subfiles.about: A final follow-up supplies corrected biographical details on Mary de Kanel and reports that nothing detrimental was known about her.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum gives Mary’s birth in Eckernförde, her English descent, marriage to Efrem de Kanel at Dalny, and immigration to the United States in 1926. It lists the couple’s children, including Nadia, Basil, and Vladimir. The inquiry ended without adverse findings.

subfiles.title: Hoover’s acknowledgment of the de Kanel investigation request
subfiles.from: John Edgar Hoover, Director, Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.to: Secretary of State, attention James Clement Dunn
subfiles.about: Hoover confirms that the FBI’s New York office has been instructed to investigate M. de Kanel.
subfiles.summary: The letter acknowledges Dunn’s April 15 request. Hoover promises to forward information as soon as it is received.

subfiles.title: File-number separator 894.20211/271
subfiles.from: Department of State records office
subfiles.about: A separator page marks file item 894.20211/271.
subfiles.summary: The page contains only the decimal-file reference. No substantive document text survives on it.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on Chinese workers and Japanese consular officers
subfiles.from: State Department, Benninghoff
subfiles.about: The sheet cross-references a report alleging collaboration between Chinese workers and Japanese consular officers in San Francisco and New York.
subfiles.summary: The underlying memorandum reportedly supplied no details about the workers’ activities. The sheet directs researchers to a separate file for the original document.

subfiles.title: Helen Wilde Alexander’s report of a suspected Japanese-interest agent
subfiles.from: Helen Wilde Alexander
subfiles.about: Alexander reports a former consular-service man in Santa Monica whom she suspects of serving Japanese interests.
subfiles.summary: She thanks Roosevelt for pardoning Dr. Townsend and recalls having previously informed Secretary Hull about secret foreign plans. Because failing eyesight required others to read her mail, she identifies Mr. Milligan of an Oakland bank as her sole trusted intermediary. She urges investigation of the Santa Monica man’s current and recent activities.

subfiles.title: Anonymous warning about Japanese visitors to steel plants
subfiles.from: Anonymous American correspondent
subfiles.about: An anonymous writer urges the government to bar Japanese visitors from steel plants in Ohio, Cleveland, and New York.
subfiles.summary: The correspondent claims that visitors arriving directly from East Asia received guided tours and manufacturing information at steel companies. The letter argues that foreign access to industrial plants is dangerous and asks Hull to intervene immediately.

subfiles.title: Charge slip for file 894.20211
subfiles.from: Department of State records office
subfiles.about: The slip records the later charging-out of decimal file 894.20211.
subfiles.summary: It supplies a date, charge number, and clerk notation. The page contains no substantive information about Japanese activity.

subfiles.title: New York citizen’s report of systematic Japanese photography
subfiles.from: C. Eaudnon
subfiles.about: A New York resident reports Japanese passengers leaving a car to photograph large buildings and landmarks in a coordinated fashion.
subfiles.summary: The writer says an unemployed friend repeatedly observed an expensive automobile carrying Japanese men to central points around the city. Once parked, the passengers allegedly dispersed with cameras and photographed buildings and landmarks, suggesting a systematic survey.

subfiles.title: Birdsey’s report of a suspected map-reading spy
subfiles.from: W. A. C. S. Birdsey
subfiles.about: Birdsey reports seeing a Japanese man at a hotel studying a map of the United States and discussing the coast near Mexico and California.
subfiles.summary: The writer interprets the map examination and conversation as evidence that the man might be a spy. He urges attention to coastal defenses and says he is reporting the incident as a patriotic duty.

subfiles.title: Milwaukee letter enclosing a marked New York transit map
subfiles.from: S. J. Brewer
subfiles.about: A Milwaukee correspondent forwards a New York rapid-transit map allegedly provided by a Japanese person.
subfiles.summary: The short letter states that the map might be significant, especially in a large city such as New York. The enclosure is an Interborough Rapid Transit map bearing a handwritten reference to Japan.

subfiles.title: Harvey A. Evans’s anti-Japanese polemic from San Francisco
subfiles.from: Harvey A. Evans
subfiles.about: Evans denounces a Japanese institution or blockhouse in San Francisco and portrays Japanese settlement as a threat to white residents and labor.
subfiles.summary: The letter presents a lengthy, openly racist account of Japanese immigration, housing acquisition, citizenship, religion, and employment practices. Evans alleges that Japanese tenants displaced white residents by exploiting landlords and charitable organizations. He frames immigration and low-wage labor as an internal war against American labor in California.

subfiles.title: Los Angeles letter reporting Japanese photography near Catalina Island
subfiles.from: Unnamed Los Angeles correspondent
subfiles.about: A Los Angeles resident reports Japanese passengers photographing the harbor and breakwater during a boat trip to Catalina Island.
subfiles.summary: The writer recalls five Japanese passengers, one of whom photographed the harbor and breakwater while the others listened to papers being read. Although conceding that investigation of the particular incident was too late, the correspondent advocates closer surveillance and harbor patrols using troops from Fort MacArthur.

subfiles.title: Newspaper clipping on Yoshio Matsuda’s harbor photography
subfiles.from: Associated Press, reprinted by the Los Angeles Times
subfiles.to: Newspaper readers; enclosed for the White House
subfiles.about: The clipping reports the detention of Japanese naval engineer Yoshio Matsuda for photographing St. Petersburg harbor.
subfiles.summary: Police and immigration officers questioned Matsuda after he photographed an area containing the USS Trenton and a Coast Guard base. Matsuda said the pictures were for personal use but acknowledged that the film would go through New York to Japan. Tokyo identified him as a lieutenant commander and naval-purchase inspector, while he declined to confirm his rank.

subfiles.title: Kilsoo K. Haan’s warning to Sumner Welles
subfiles.from: Kilsoo K. Haan, Sino-Korean Peoples’ League
subfiles.to: Sumner Welles, Under Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Haan warns that a possible understanding involving Japan could harm Pacific security and recalls earlier intelligence supplied by his organization.
subfiles.summary: The handwritten letter refers to previous informational submissions and to international intrigue that had already passed without sufficient attention. Haan fears that a new understanding between countries would be detrimental to the security and stability of the Pacific.

subfiles.title: Sino-Korean Peoples’ League press release on Japanese cultural propaganda
subfiles.from: Kilsoo K. Haan, Sino-Korean Peoples’ League
subfiles.about: Haan alleges that Japan planned to spend three million yen influencing American colleges, churches, educators, and students.
subfiles.summary: The release identifies Dale D. Welch and Katsu Koike and claims that at least 300 educators and churchmen would be recruited. It accuses the American Council, Institute of Pacific Relations, of facilitating the program and recalls an earlier dispute over allegedly Japanized textbooks in Hawaii and New York. Haan threatens to seek a Dies Committee investigation.

subfiles.title: Congressional Record: “Congress Wants Peace—Japan Wants P-I-E-C-E”
subfiles.from: Vincent F. Harrington and Kilsoo K. Haan
subfiles.about: Harrington inserts Haan’s appeal for abrogation of the 1911 commercial treaty with Japan into the Congressional Record.
subfiles.summary: Haan alleges that Japanese ronin were being sent to Shanghai to terrorize foreigners and cites incidents involving American property, personnel, and Japanese activity in Hawaii. He argues that Japanese expansion threatened American interests, democracy, and labor standards throughout the Pacific. The letter urges Congress to support Senator Vandenberg’s treaty-abrogation resolution.

subfiles.title: Duplicate Sino-Korean Peoples’ League press release
subfiles.from: Kilsoo K. Haan, Sino-Korean Peoples’ League
subfiles.about: A second copy alleges a Japanese campaign to influence American colleges, churches, educators, and students.
subfiles.summary: The text repeats the claim that Japan allocated three million yen to promote sympathetic understanding of its new order in Asia. It again names Dale D. Welch, Katsu Koike, the American Council, and the earlier textbook controversy. A State Department filing stamp shows that this copy was separately received and retained.

subfiles.title: Duplicate Congressional Record excerpt on Japan
subfiles.from: Vincent F. Harrington and Kilsoo K. Haan
subfiles.about: A second copy reproduces Haan’s congressional appeal against Japanese expansion and for treaty abrogation.
subfiles.summary: The excerpt repeats allegations about ronin in Shanghai, Japanese activities in Hawaii, and assaults on American interests in China. It urges Congress to resist Japan’s acquisition of American interests “by pieces” and support Senator Vandenberg’s resolution.

subfiles.title: White House-referred copy of the Japanese propaganda press release
subfiles.from: Kilsoo K. Haan, Sino-Korean Peoples’ League
subfiles.to: The press; referred by the White House to the Department of State
subfiles.about: A further copy of Haan’s press release reached the State Department through a White House referral.
subfiles.summary: It repeats allegations of a three-million-yen Japanese propaganda program in American educational and religious institutions. The release again links the plan to Dale D. Welch, Katsu Koike, and the Institute of Pacific Relations and recalls the earlier textbook campaign.

subfiles.title: Third Congressional Record copy on Japanese expansion
subfiles.from: Vincent F. Harrington and Kilsoo K. Haan
subfiles.about: A third retained copy reproduces Haan’s appeal for action against Japanese expansion and interference with American interests.
subfiles.summary: The document again cites threats in Shanghai, attacks on American property and personnel, and Japanese mobilization in Hawaii. It presents abrogation of the 1911 treaty as a warning to Japanese militarists and as support for Chinese, Korean, and liberal Japanese elements.

subfiles.title: Sino-Korean Peoples’ League petition to Philip C. Jessup
subfiles.from: Kilsoo K. Haan, Sino-Korean Peoples’ League
subfiles.to: Philip C. Jessup, Institute of Pacific Relations
subfiles.about: Haan petitions Jessup to investigate Institute of Pacific Relations policies allegedly aiding Japanese cultural propaganda in the United States and Hawaii.
subfiles.summary: The petition alleges that Inazo Nitobe’s survey of American opinion encouraged Japanese aggression and that Setsuichi Aoki, Kanekazu Okada, and Viscount Ishii developed cultural programs designed to Japanize American children and Japanese Americans. It reviews disputes over school textbooks, proposed propaganda in colleges and churches, Ernest O. Hauser’s alleged advice, and the growth of Japanese-language schools in Hawaii. Haan also protests the exclusion of Korean representatives from Institute conferences and argues that democracy, Korean representation, and resistance to Japanese militarism are essential to Pacific peace.

subfiles.title: Duplicate petition to Philip C. Jessup, incomplete in this section
